contenido: To the venerable brother patriarchs, primates, archbishops and bishops of the entire world who have grace and communion with the Apostolic See

How much diligence and pastoral vigilance the Roman Pontiffs, Our Predecessors, have employed without interruption, in fulfilling the office that the Lord Christ Himself entrusted to them in the person of the blessed Peter, Prince of the Apostles, and the charge of feeding the lambs and the sheep, in diligently nourishing the entire flock of the Lord with words of faith and imbuing it with healthy doctrine and in separating it from poisonous pastures, is a well-known and experienced by everyone and especially by you, Venerable Brothers. And in truth, those same Predecessors of Ours, defenders and avengers of the most august Catholic religion, of truth and justice, extremely solicitous for the salvation of souls, never considered anything more preferable than to discover and condemn, with their most wise Letters and Constitutions, all the heresies and errors that, contrary to our divine faith, to the doctrine of the Catholic Church, to the honesty of customs and to the everlasting salvation of men, They frequently caused serious storms and pitifully devastated the Christian and civil republic. Therefore, those same Predecessors of Ours, with apostolic strength, continually opposed the nefarious machinations of wicked men, who, vomiting up their confusions like waves of the rough sea and promising freedom while being servants of corruption, with their fallacious opinions and very pernicious writings attempted to uproot the foundations of the Catholic religion and civil society, to remove all virtue and justice from the midst, to deprave the souls and minds of all and, above all, to separate the unwary and inexperienced youth from the correct discipline of customs, to corrupt them miserably, to lead them into the bonds of error and, finally, to tear them from the bosom of the Catholic Church.

You already know well, Venerable Brothers, that only by the arcane design of divine providence and without any merit of Our own were elevated to this Chair of Peter, when, seeing with the utmost pain of Our soul the horrible storm raised by so many perverse opinions and the very serious and never sufficiently mourned damages that are derived from so many errors to the Christian people, out of the duty of Our Apostolic Ministry and following in the illustrious footsteps of Our Predecessors, We raised Our voice and, In several published Encyclicals, in Addresses delivered in the Consistory and in other Apostolic Letters, we condemn the main errors of our very sad era, we encourage your excellent episcopal vigilance and we admonish and exhort again and again all the children of the Catholic Church, Our dearest ones, to completely abhor and avoid the contagion of such a fatal plague. And in a special way in Our first Encyclical Letter, written to you on November 9, 1846, and in two Addresses, one of which was delivered by Us in the Consistory on December 9, 1854 and the other on June 9, 1862, we condemn monstrous portents of opinions that at this time above all dominate with maximum damage to souls and to the detriment of civil society itself, and that are not only They oppose in the highest degree not only the Catholic Church, its healthy doctrine and its venerable rights, but also the everlasting natural law carved by God in the hearts of all and right reason, and from which almost all other errors originate.

Although we have not omitted to frequently condemn and reprove the main ones of such errors, nevertheless the cause of the Catholic Church, the salvation of souls entrusted to Us by God and the good of human society itself completely demand that we once again excite your pastoral concern to combat other perverse opinions that spring from those same errors as from sources. Such false and perverse opinions are all the more detestable as they aim above all to impede and remove that salutary force which the Catholic Church, by institution and mandate of its divine Author, must exercise freely until the consummation of the centuries, no less with respect to individual men than to nations, peoples and their supreme Princes, and to remove from the middle that mutual partnership and concord of counsel between the Priesthood and the Empire which was always favorable and salutary to both the sacred and the civil (1). In fact, you well know, Venerable Brothers, that at this time there are not a few who, applying to civil society the impious and absurd principle of naturalism, as they call it, dare to teach that "the optimal reason for public society and civil progress completely demand that human society be constituted and governed without taking religion into account at all, as if it did not exist, or at least without making any discrimination between true and false religions." And, against the doctrine of the sacred Letters, the Church and the holy Fathers, they do not hesitate to affirm that "the optimal condition of society is that in which the Empire is not recognized as having the office of restricting violators of the Catholic religion with sanctioned penalties, except as far as public peace postulates it." From this completely false idea of the social regime, they are not afraid to promote that erroneous opinion, extremely harmful to the Catholic Church and to the salvation of souls, called delirium by Our predecessor of happy memory Gregory XVI (2), namely: that "freedom of conscience and worship is the right of every man, which must be proclaimed and affirmed by law in every rightly constituted society, and that citizens are entitled to the right to all freedom, not restricted by any ecclesiastical authority or civil, to manifest and declare openly and in public any of his concepts, whether by word of mouth, or by print, or in any other way. And while they recklessly affirm this, they do not think or consider that they preach freedom from perdition (3), and that if "it were always free to dispute with human persuasions, there will never be a shortage of those who dare to resist the truth and trust in the folly of human wisdom, Christian faith and wisdom having to avoid this most ignorant vanity, as it knows from the very institution of Our Lord Jesus Christ" (4).

And since, where religion has been distanced from civil society and the doctrine and authority of divine revelation has been repudiated, even the very genuine notion of justice and human right is obscured with darkness and is lost, and in the place of true justice and legitimate right material force is substituted, it is clearly understood why some, completely despising and postponing the most certain principles of sound reason, dare to loudly proclaim that "the will of the people, manifested by so-called public opinion or otherwise, constitutes the supreme law, detached from all divine and human rights, and that in the political order accomplished facts, by the mere fact of being accomplished, have the force of law. But who does not clearly see and feel that the society of men, separated from the bonds of religion and true justice, can truly propose no other goal than that of acquiring and accumulating wealth, nor follow in its actions any law other than the indomitable desire of the spirit to serve its own pleasures and comforts? That is why such men persecute with bitter hatred the Religious Families, although extremely deserving of the Christian, civil and literary cause, and stammer that they have no legitimate reason to exist, and thus applaud the inventions of heretics. For, as Our Predecessor of happy memory Pius VI wisely taught, "the abolition of the Regulars hurts the state of the public profession of the evangelical councils, it hurts a way of life recommended in the Church as in accordance with apostolic doctrine, it hurts the distinguished Founders themselves, whom we venerate on the altars, and who only inspired by God constituted these societies" (5). And they also impiously pronounce that the power of the Church "by which they can openly dispense alms for the sake of Christian charity" must be taken away from citizens, and that the law "by which on certain days servile works are prohibited for the worship of God" must be removed from the way, very fallaciously pretexting that the aforementioned power and law are opposed to the optimal principles of public economy. And not content with removing religion from public society, they also want to remove the same religion from private families. In fact, teaching and professing the very fatal error of Communism and socialism, they affirm that “the domestic society or family takes the entire reason for its existence from civil law alone; and therefore that only all the rights of parents over their children arise and depend on civil law, and first of all the right to take care of their instruction and education. With these impious opinions and machinations, these most deceitful men aim above all to completely eliminate from the instruction and education of youth the healthy doctrine and strength of the Catholic Church, and that the tender and flexible spirits of the young become miserably infected and depraved with any errors and pernicious vices. For all those who have tried to disturb the sacred and the public, upset the right order of society and destroy all divine and human rights, have always dedicated, as we hinted above, all their nefarious advice, studies and work to deceive and deprave, above all, improvident youth, and in the corruption of that same youth they placed all their hope. For this reason they never cease to humiliate in so many infamous ways both the clergy, from which, as the most reliable monuments of history splendidly attest, so many great benefits have been derived to the Christian, civil and literary republic, and to proclaim that the same Clergy, "as an enemy of the true and useful progress of science and civilization, must be removed from all care and office of instructing and educating youth."

But others, renewing the perverse and infinitely condemned inventions of the innovators, with marked impudence dare to subject to the discretion of the civil authority the supreme authority of the Church and of this Apostolic See, entrusted to it by Christ the Lord, and to deny all the rights of that same Church and See in what concerns the external order. For they are not at all ashamed to affirm that "the laws of the Church are not binding in conscience except when they are promulgated by the civil power; that the acts and decrees of the Roman Pontiffs relating to religion and the Church need the sanction and approval, or at least the assent, of the civil power; that the Apostolic constitutions (6) by which clandestine societies are condemned, whether or not they require an oath of secrecy, and their followers and supporters are punished with anathema, have no force whatsoever in those regions of the world where such aggregations are tolerated by the civil government; that the excommunication carried out by the Council of Trent and by the Roman Pontiffs against those who invade and usurp the rights and possessions of the Church is based on the confusion of the spiritual order and the civil and political order, pursued only for worldly good; that the Church should decree nothing that could bind the consciences of the faithful in the order of use of temporal things; that the Church does not have the right to restrict violators of its laws with temporary penalties; that it is in accordance with the principles of sacred theology and public law to attribute and claim for the civil government the ownership of the property owned by the Church, religious families and other pious places. And they do not blush to openly and publicly profess the saying and principle of the heretics, from which so many perverse sentences and errors originate. For they repeat that "ecclesiastical power is not by divine right distinct and independent from civil power, nor can such distinction and independence be preserved without the Church invading and usurping the essential rights of civil power." And we cannot pass in silence the audacity of those who, not upholding sound doctrine, affirm that "to those judgments and decrees of the Apostolic See whose object is declared to concern the general good of the Church and its rights and discipline, as long as they do not touch the dogmas of faith and customs, assent and obedience can be refused without sin and without any impairment of the Catholic profession." How much this opposes the Catholic dogma of the full power divinely entrusted by Christ the Lord himself to the Roman Pontiff to universally feed, rule and govern the Church, there is no one who does not see and understand it clearly and openly.

In so much perversity of depraved opinions, We, remembering Our apostolic office and extremely solicitous of Our most holy religion, of the sound doctrine and of the salvation of souls entrusted to Us by God, and of the good of human society itself, We have deemed it appropriate to raise Our apostolic voice again. Therefore, with Our apostolic authority We reprove, proscribe and condemn each and every one of the perverse opinions and doctrines singularly remembered in these Letters, and we want and command that by all the children of the Catholic Church they be considered completely reprobated, proscribed and condemned.

And in addition to this, you know very well, Venerable Brothers, that in these times all the haters of all truth and justice and the staunch enemies of our religion, through pestiferous books, libels and newspapers spread throughout the entire globe of the earth, mocking the people and lying maliciously, disseminate any other impious doctrines. Nor are you unaware that in this age of ours there are also some who, moved and incited by the spirit of Satan, have reached such a degree of impiety that they are not afraid to deny Our Lord Jesus Christ, the Dominator, and attack His Divinity with criminal profanity. Here we can only praise you with maximum and well-deserved praise, Venerable Brothers, who with all zeal have not omitted to raise your episcopal voice against so much impiety.

Therefore, with these Our Letters, We once again speak with great kindness to you, who, called to participate in Our concern, are for Us, in the midst of Our greatest bitterness, the utmost consolation, joy and consolation for the egregious religion and piety in which you excel and for that admirable love, faith and observance with which, united to Us and to this Apostolic See with the most concordant spirits, you strive to fulfill with energy and diligence your very serious episcopal ministry. In fact, from your excellent pastoral zeal we hope that, taking up the sword of the spirit, which is the word of God, and comforted by the grace of Our Lord Jesus Christ, you will want with redoubled efforts to provide more and more every day so that the faithful entrusted to your care "abstain from the harmful herbs that Jesus Christ does not cultivate, because they are not the Father's plantation" (7). And never cease to instill in those same faithful that all true happiness is derived to men from our most august religion, from its doctrine and its exercise, and that blessed are the people whose Lord is their God (8). Teach that "on the foundation of the Catholic faith the kingdoms subsist (9), and that there is nothing so deadly, so precipitate towards fall, so exposed to all dangers, as if, thinking that only that which we received at birth, free will, was enough for us, we no longer sought anything more from the Lord, that is, forgetting our author, we abjured his power to show ourselves free" (10). And do not omit to teach that the royal power is not conferred only for the rule of the world, but above all for the protection of the Church (11), and that nothing can be of greater fruit and glory to the Princes and Kings of the cities who, as Our most wise and strong Predecessor Saint Felix wrote to Emperor Zeno, "allow the Catholic Church... to use its own laws, and do not allow anyone to oppose its freedom... Well, it is true that this is salutary to their affairs: that, when dealing with the causes of God, according to the constitution of Himself they strive to submit the royal will to the Priests of Christ, not to put it before it" (12).

But always, Venerable Brothers, now especially, in so many calamities of the Church and civil society, in such a great conspiracy of the adversaries against the Catholic cause and this Apostolic See and in such a great accumulation of errors, it is absolutely necessary that we approach the throne of Grace with confidence, to obtain mercy and find grace in timely help. For this reason we have deemed it appropriate to excite the piety of all the faithful so that, together with Us and with you, they pray and pray without intermission with the most fervent and most humble prayers to the most merciful Father of lights and mercies, and in the fullness of faith they always take refuge in Our Lord Jesus Christ, who redeemed us for God with His blood, and in His most sweet Heart, victim of the most ardent charity towards us, Pray without ceasing and earnestly, so that with the bonds of your love you may draw all things to yourself, and so that all men, inflamed with your most holy love, may walk according to your Heart, worthily pleasing God in everything, bearing fruit in every good work. And since, without a doubt, the prayers of men are more pleasing to God if they approach Him with minds purified of all stain, therefore We have deemed it appropriate to open with apostolic liberality to the faithful of Christ the heavenly treasures of the Church entrusted to Our dispensation, so that those same faithful, more vehemently inflamed to true piety and purified from the stains of sins by the Sacrament of Penance, pour out their prayers to God with greater confidence and reach his mercy and grace.

Therefore, with these Letters, by Our apostolic authority, We grant to all the faithful of both sexes of the Catholic world Plenary Indulgence as a Jubilee, within the space of a single month that you, Venerable Brothers, and the other legitimate Ordinaries of the places must determine, until the entire coming year of 1865 and not beyond, in the same way and form in which We granted it from the beginning of Our supreme Pontificate for Our Apostolic Letters in the form of a Brief, given on the 20th of November of the year 1846 and sent to your entire Episcopal Order, whose beginning is "Arcano Divinae Providentiae consilio", and with all the same faculties that were given by Us through those same Letters. We want, however, that everything prescribed in the aforementioned Letters be observed, and that what we declare excepted be excepted. And we grant this without obstructing any things that do the contrary, even if they are worthy of special and individual mention and repeal. And so that all doubt and difficulty may be removed, we have ordered that a copy of those same Letters be brought to you.

«We pray, Venerable Brothers, from the depths of our hearts and with all our minds, the mercy of God, because He Himself added saying: But I will not scatter my mercy from them. Let us ask and we will receive, and if there is delay or delay in receiving, because we have seriously offended, let us knock, because to him who knocks it will also be opened, provided that our prayers, groans and tears knock at the door, in which it is advisable to insist and linger, and if the prayer is unanimous... let each one pray to God not only for himself, but for all his brothers, as the Lord taught us to pray (13)." And so that God may more easily grant Our prayers and yours and those of all the faithful, and their vows, with all confidence let us take as intercessor before Him the Immaculate and most holy Mother of God Virgin Mary, who exterminated all heresies throughout the world, and who, the most loving Mother of us all, "is all gentle... and full of mercy... she shows herself to all exorable, to all most merciful, and has compassion for the needs of all with a very broad affection (14)»; and, as a Queen who is at the right hand of her Only Begotten Son, Our Lord Jesus Christ in a dress of gold, surrounded by variety, there is nothing that she cannot achieve from Him. Let us also ask for the suffrages of the blessed Peter, Prince of the Apostles, and of his Co-Apostle Paul, and of all the Saints in heaven, who, now friends of God, have reached the heavenly kingdoms and, crowned, possess the palm and, assured of their immortality, are solicitous for our salvation.

Finally, sincerely wishing you from God the abundance of all heavenly gifts, as a pledge of Our singular charity towards you, We lovingly impart the Apostolic Blessing, coming from the depths of our hearts, to yourselves, Venerable Brothers, and to all the clerics and lay faithful entrusted to your care.
Given in Rome, next to Saint Peter, on December 8, 1864, tenth since the Dogmatic Definition of the Immaculate Conception of the Mother of God Virgin Mary.
(6) Clement XII, In eminenti; Benedict XIV, Providas Romanorum; Pius VII, Ecclesiam; Leo XII, Quo graviora.
IN THE CONSISTORIAL ADDRESSES, IN THE ENCYCLICALS AND IN OTHER APOSTOLIC LETTERS OF OUR HOLY LORD POPE PIO IX.

I. There is no supreme divine Numen, most wise and most provident, distinct from this universality of things, and God is the same as the nature of things and, therefore, is subject to changes; and God is truly made in man and in the world, and all things are God and have the very substance of God; and God is the same thing with the world, and therefore the spirit with matter, necessity with freedom, the true with the false, the good with the evil and the just with the unjust.

III. Human reason, without taking God into account at all, is the only arbiter of what is true and what is false, of good and evil; It is a law unto itself, and with its natural forces it is sufficient to ensure the good of men and peoples.
IV. All the truths of religion derive from the native force of human reason; hence reason is the main norm by which man can and should achieve knowledge of all truths of any kind.
V. Divine revelation is imperfect and, therefore, is subject to a continuous and indefinite progress that corresponds to the progress of human reason.
VI. The faith of Christ is opposed to human reason; and divine revelation not only is of no avail, but even harms the perfection of man.

VII. The prophecies and miracles exposed and narrated in the sacred Letters are inventions of poets, and the mysteries of the Christian faith are the compendium of philosophical investigations; and in the books of both Testaments mythical inventions are contained; and Jesus Christ himself is a mythical fiction.
VIII. Since human reason is equated with religion itself, theological disciplines must be treated in the same way as philosophical ones.

IX. All the dogmas of the Christian religion, without distinction, are the object of natural science or philosophy; and human reason, cultivated only historically, can with its natural forces and principles arrive at the true science of all dogmas, even the most recondite ones, provided that these dogmas have been proposed to reason as an object.

X. Since the philosopher is one thing and philosophy another, the former has the right and duty to submit to the authority that he himself has proven to be true; but philosophy neither can nor should submit to any authority.
XI. The Church should not only never intervene in philosophy, but should tolerate the errors of philosophy itself and let it correct itself.
XII. The decrees of the Apostolic See and the Roman Congregations prevent the free progress of science.
XIII. The method and principles with which the ancient scholastic doctors cultivated Theology are in no way adapted to the needs of our times or to the progress of science.
XIV. Philosophy must be treated without taking into account supernatural revelation.

N. B. — The errors of Antonio Günther, which are condemned in the Epistle to the Cardinal Archbishop of Cologne Eximiam tuam, of June 15, 1857, and in the Epistle to the Bishop of Breslau Dolore haud mediocri, of April 30, 1860, coincide for the most part with the system of rationalism.
XV. Every man is free to embrace and profess that religion which, guided by the light of reason, he has judged to be true.
XVI. Men can find the way to eternal salvation and achieve eternal salvation in the worship of any religion.
XVII. At least good is to be expected from the eternal salvation of all those who are in no way in the true Church of Christ.
XVIII. Protestantism is nothing other than a different form of the same true Christian religion, in which, as in the Catholic Church, pleasing God has been given.
§ IV. Socialism, Communism, Clandestine societies, Biblical societies, Clerical-liberal societies

Such plagues are often reproached and with very serious formulas of words in the encyclical Epistle Qui pluribus, of November 9, 1846; in the Allocution Quibus quantisque, April 20, 1849; in the encyclical Epistle Nostis et Nobiscum, December 8, 1849; in the Allocution Singulari quadam, December 9, 1854; in the encyclical Epistle Quanto conficiamur, August 10, 1863.

XIX. The Church is not a true and perfect society, completely free, nor does it enjoy its own and constant rights conferred by its divine Founder, but it is up to the civil power to define what the rights of the Church are and the limits within which it can exercise those same rights.
XX. The ecclesiastical power must not exercise its authority without the permission and assent of the civil government.
XXI. The Church does not have the power to dogmatically define that the religion of the Catholic Church is the only true religion.

XXII. The obligation to which Catholic teachers and writers are subject at all points is limited only to those things that, by the infallible judgment of the Church, are proposed to all as dogmas of faith to be believed.
XXIII. The Roman Pontiffs and the Ecumenical Councils went beyond the limits of their power, usurped the rights of princes and even erred in defining matters of faith and customs.
XXIV. The Church has no power to use force, nor any temporal power, direct or indirect.

XXV. In addition to the power inherent to the episcopate, there is another temporal power attributed, granted expressly or tacitly by the civil empire, and therefore revocable at will by the civil empire.
XXVII. The sacred ministers of the Church and the Roman Pontiff are to be completely excluded from all care and control of temporal things.
XXVIII. Bishops, without permission from the government, are not allowed to promulgate even the Apostolic Letters themselves.
XXIX. The graces granted by the Roman Pontiff must be considered null, unless they have been implored by the government.
XXX. The immunity of the Church and ecclesiastical persons had its origin in civil law.

XXXI. The ecclesiastical jurisdiction for the temporal causes of clerics, whether civil or criminal, must be completely removed from the way, even without consulting the Apostolic See and claiming it.

XXXII. Without any violation of natural law and equity, personal immunity can be abrogated by which clerics are exempt from the burden of supporting and exercising the militia; and this abrogation is postulated by civil progress, especially in a society constituted as a freer regime.
XXXIII. It does not belong solely to the power of ecclesiastical jurisdiction, by its own and native right, to direct the doctrine of theological things.
XXXIV. The doctrine of those who compare the Roman Pontiff with a free Prince who acts in the universal Church is a doctrine that prevailed in the Middle Ages.

XXXV. Nothing prevents the Supreme Pontificate from being transferred from the Roman Bishop and the City to another Bishop and to another city, by ruling of some general Council or by act of the universal peoples.
XXXVI. The definition of a national Council does not admit another dispute, and the civil administration can demand the matter under these terms.
XXXVII. National Churches can be established, removed from the authority of the Roman Pontiff and completely divided.
XXXVIII. The excessive discretions of the Roman Pontiffs contributed to the division of the Church into eastern and western.
§VI. Errors about civil society considered in itself and in its relations with the Church
XXXIX. The State of the republic, as the origin and source of all rights, enjoys a right not circumscribed by any limits.
XL. The doctrine of the Catholic Church is opposed to the good and conveniences of human society.

XLI. Civil power, even exercised by an unfaithful ruler, has a negative indirect power in the sacred; Therefore, it is responsible not only for the so-called right of “exequatur”, but also for the right of the so-called “appeal for abuse”.

XLIII. The lay power has the authority to rescind, declare and invalidate the solemn conventions (vulgo Concordats) celebrated with the Apostolic See on the use of the rights belonging to ecclesiastical immunity, without its consent and even claiming it.

XLIV. The civil authority can interfere in things that belong to religion, customs and spiritual regime. Hence he can judge the instructions that the pastors of the Church give, by their office, as a norm of conscience, and he can even decree about the administration of the divine sacraments and the necessary dispositions to receive them.

XLV. The entire regime of the public schools in which the youth of a Christian Republic is educated, with the sole exception in some way of the episcopal seminaries, can and must be attributed to the civil authority, and in such a way attributed that no other authority is recognized the right to interfere in the discipline of the schools, in the regime of studies, in the collation of degrees, in the election or approval of teachers.
XLVI. What's more: in the cleric seminaries themselves, the method of study to be used is subject to civil authority.

XLVII. The optimal reason for civil society postulates that the popular schools, open to children of all classes of the people, and in general the public institutes destined for the teaching of letters and the most severe disciplines and for the care of the education of youth, are exempt from all authority, moderating force and interference of the Church, and are subject to the full discretion of the civil and political authority, according to the taste of the rulers and to the extent of the common opinions of the time.

XLVIII. The reason for instituting youth that is separated from the Catholic faith and the power of the Church, and that looks only, or at least mainly, to the science of natural things and the ends of earthly social life, can be approved by Catholic men.
XLIX. The civil authority can prevent the sacred Antistites and the faithful peoples from communicating freely and mutually with the Roman Pontiff.

L. The lay authority has in itself the right to present the Bishops and can demand that they assume the oversight of the dioceses before receiving the canonical institution and the Apostolic Letters from the Holy See.

LI. Furthermore: the lay government has the right to depose the Bishops from the exercise of pastoral ministry, and is not obliged to obey the Roman Pontiff with regard to the institution of bishoprics and Bishops.

LII. The government may by its right change the age prescribed by the Church for the religious profession of women and men, and order all religious families not to admit anyone to pronounce solemn vows without their permission.

LIII. The laws that concern protecting the state of religious families and their rights and offices must be repealed; Furthermore, the civil government can provide assistance to all those who want to desert the institute of religious life that they assumed and break their solemn vows; and in the same way it can completely extinguish those same religious families, as well as the collegiate churches and simple benefits, including the right of patronage, and subject and vindicate their assets and income to the administration and discretion of the civil power.
LIV. Kings and Princes are not only exempt from the jurisdiction of the Church, but they are also superior to the Church in matters of jurisdiction that must be settled.
LVI. The laws of customs do not need divine sanction, and it is in no way necessary that human laws conform to the law of nature or receive the force of binding from God.
LVII. The sciences of philosophical things and customs, and also civil laws, can and must decline from divine and ecclesiastical authority.

LVIII. No other forces are to be recognized except those that are placed in the matter, and all discipline of customs and honesty must be placed on accumulating and increasing wealth in any way and fulfilling pleasures.
LIX. Law consists of the material fact, and all the offices of men are a vain name, and all human acts have the force of law.

LXIV. Both the violation of the most sacred oath and any criminal and flagitious action repugnant to the everlasting law, not only is it not to be condemned, but it is completely lawful and worthy of the utmost praise when done for love of the country.
LXV. In no way can it be admitted that Christ elevated marriage to the dignity of a sacrament.
LXVI. The sacrament of marriage is nothing but something accessory to the contract and separable from it, and the sacrament itself consists only of the nuptial blessing alone.
LXVII. By the law of nature the bond of marriage is not indissoluble, and in several cases the divorce itself can be sanctioned by the civil authority.
LXVIII. The Church does not have the power to introduce settling impediments to marriage, but that power belongs to the civil authority, from which the existing impediments must be removed.
LXIX. In subsequent centuries, the Church began to introduce settling impediments not by its own right, but by using that right that it had borrowed from civil power.

LXX. The Tridentine canons that make censorship anathema to those who dare to deny the Church the power to introduce decisive impediments, are either not dogmatic or must be understood from this borrowed power.
LXXI. The Tridentine form does not bind under penalty of nullity where the civil law prescribes another form and wants that, by intervening in this new form, the marriage is valid.
LXXII. Boniface VIII was the first to affirm that the vow of chastity cast at ordination renders nuptials null and void.

LXXIII. By virtue of a purely civil contract, a real name marriage can be established between Christians, and it is false that the marriage contract between Christians is always a sacrament, or that there is no contract if the sacrament is excluded.
LXXIV. Matrimonial cases and betrothals per se belong to the civil jurisdiction.

N.B. — Two other errors may be relevant here: that of abolishing the celibacy of clerics and that of putting the state of marriage before the state of virginity. They are confused, the first in the Encyclical Epistle Qui pluribus, of November 9, 1846; the second in the Apostolic Letters Multiplices inter, of June 10, 1851.
LXXV. The children of the Christian and Catholic Church dispute among themselves the compatibility of the temporal kingdom with the spiritual one.
LXXVI. The abrogation of the civil empire enjoyed by the Apostolic See would lead to the maximum degree to the freedom and happiness of the Church.

N. B. — Sayings on this matter see also the Allocution Quibus quantisque, of April 20, 1849; in the Address Si semper antea, May 20, 1850; in the Apostolic Letters Cum catholica, of March 26, 1860; in the Novos Address, September 28, 1860; in the Allocution Multis gravibusque, December 17, 1860; in the Allocution Maxima quidem, June 9, 1862.
LXXVII. In this age of ours it is no longer appropriate for the Catholic religion to be the only religion of the State, to the exclusion of any other cults.
LXXVIII. Hence, laudably, it has been provided by law in some regions with a Catholic name that men who emigrate to them are allowed to have the public exercise of their proper worship.

LXXIX. In fact, it is false that the civil freedom of any religion, and also the full power attributed to everyone to openly and publicly express any opinions and thoughts, leads to more easily corrupting the customs and spirits of people and spreading the plague of indifferentism.
LXXX. The Roman Pontiff can and must reconcile and reconcile himself with progress, with liberalism and with recent civilization.
H. Denzinger, Enchiridion symbolorum definitionum et declarationum de rebus fidei et morum, 43rd ed. bilingual, by Peter Hünermann, Centro editoriale dehoniano, Bologna, 2012, p. 1024-1041.
